newsitem.title: UK: Transport could be key battleground in UK election.
newsitem.headline: Transport could be key battleground in UK election.

text.p: Transport is seen as one of the possible battlegrounds on which Britain's May 1 election will be fought as the country faces the threat of a traffic gridlock unless changes are made to the nationwide transport system.

The British transport sector offers the opposition Labour party, widely expected to win the right to form the next government, the opportunity and challenge of revamping the system which has drawn widespread criticism amongst the country's commuters.

With many votes seen riding on transport policy -- particularly in London where the cash-starved underground rail system is creating commuter misery -- Labour's shadow transport secretary Andrew Smith and his deputy, the Oscar-winning ex-actress Glenda Jackson, made a high-profile launch of their blueprint for change in February.
The Smith and Jackson double-act has been welcomed by relieved transport industry chiefs who see them as more pragmatic than Labour predecessor Clare Short who had a more interventionist approach.
But the main uncertainty for transport lies in shadow Chancellor Gordon Brown's proposed windfall tax on privatised utilities.
Recent press speculation suggest that a Labour government will fund part of its political programme through the tax.

So far Labour has refused to define which companies will be caught in the net, but some press reports have suggested the net has been widened to raise up to 10 billion pounds, double the original estimate.

Transport companies which could be hit include the airport operator BAA Plc, Associated British Ports Plc, the recently privatised rail infrastructure group Railtrack Plc and possibly the rail rolling stock leasing companies (known as ROSCOs) which are seen as cash-cows.
Britain's privatised bus network, sold off by regions in a process which began 10 years ago, has less of a tax target.
The other possible threat a Labour victory poses is a tougher regulatory regime which is likely to be harder on rail than buses.
In an interview with Reuters in early March, Labour's Smith said he planned a rail regulatory system with bite, citing Railtrack and the passenger franchises as targets.

He said he would use existing powers to force Railtrack to meet investment obligations. This could be done by tightening its 2001 price review or amending its track access conditions which govern payments to Railtrack for use of its infrastructure.
As a last resort, Labour could use primary legislation to impose minimum investment levels on Railtrack.
Railtrack, sold off last year, has been singled out for criticism for failing to meet investment pledges.

Labour's Smith sent a warning shot in the interview. "There is already a 700 million backlog. Railtrack is a national monopoly and its investment is critical nationwide. We certainly won't be deflected by any delaying tactics which may be used by Railtrack."

On wider regulatory issues, Labour's Smith could merge the Office of Passenger Rail Franchising (Opraf) with the rail regulator creating a super-powerful transport watchdog. This could also govern buses.
On buses, Smith has moved away from his predecessor's policy of a tough and prescriptive regulatory regime on issues like fare structure.

Instead, Labour is seen reviewing competition law to see if changes are needed to allow bus firms to collaborate where it is in the interests of the passenger -- on issues like timetabling and ticketing.

A Labour government would not be a road-building government. Instead, Smith said he is committed to traffic management by getting more passengers out of cars and onto the transport network and using rail to carry freight rather than lorries.
But Labour leader, Tony Blair, has stopped short of attacking car owners and the car industry -- a major jobs creator -- telling the transport Industry Forum conference in February:
"I am not interested in demonising the car. The focus of government policy needs to be offering people attractive alternatives to using their car."

On the future of the London Underground -- seen as a potential vote winner in the capital by both Labour and the ruling Conservative Party -- Blair says there will no sell-off if it wins the election.
The ruling Conservatives plan a London Underground privatisation which is seen raising up tap two billion.
But Labour intends to revitalise the metro system by encouraging more private sector capital into the network on tunnel maintenance, track, signalling and trains.
Labour is also looking at an electronic swipe smart-card for use across the tube network which could possibly be extended to rail, buses, taxis and even retail outlets at transport stations.
